source.version_note: Supplied publisher article in Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 111 (2024), article 104582. Front matter explicitly says available online 19 December 2023; use issue citation year 2024 while retaining the online-2023 version history. The front-matter label Case Report does not turn the three vignette experiments into a clinical case report.
source.verification_method: All eight extracted-text pages read, including references. Figures 1–4 and Tables 1–2 visually inspected on PDF pages 3–7. Main identity and two wrong-DOI replacements checked against Crossref. No OSF data/code, supplementary study or full cited primary paper was independently read or reproduced.

citation.title: Hazardous machinery: The assignment of agency and blame to robots versus non-autonomous machines

reading.source_scope_note: Three online vignette experiments with 570 retained participations in total, plus a separately reported capability-description pretest of 45. Human perceptions of fictional accidents and a military robot are measured; no actual robot behavior, fault investigation, legal judgment or conscious machine state is tested.
access_limits: Supplementary Study A, OSF materials, raw data, exclusions, code and exact item sets were not independently read or reproduced. A view-only token printed in the PDF is deliberately not copied to the public review.
Cited primary mind-perception, mediation and robot studies were not fully reread. Bibliographic identity checks are metadata only and do not receive independent full-review credit.
Actual machine control, intent, injury cause and capabilities are not independently established by the vignette labels. Cross-study participant uniqueness is not documented.

study.design: Studies 1 and 2 cross autonomous-robot versus machine labels with 24 accident contexts. Each participant sees eight unique contexts, four of each label, in random order. The 48 possible vignettes are not 48 independent samples. Study 3 uses a between-person more/less sophisticated armed bi-pedal/humanoid ABTAC robot description, followed by a fatality vignette.
study.samples: Study 1 requests 144, receives 147 and excludes two attention failures, retaining 145 (94 women, 49 men, two other; mean age 38.09, SD 13.20). Study 2 requests 144, replaces ten attention failures and retains 143 (97 women, 46 men; age 40.08, SD 12.89). Study 3 requests 280, replaces 52 attention failures and retains 282 (178 women, 100 men, three other, one unreported; age 38.9, SD 13.41). These sum to 570 retained participations, not verified unique individuals. Convenience North American/UK internet samples recruited via Prolific.
study.measures: Agency: six items including self-control and ability to influence outcomes; alphas .86/.84/.81. Studies 1/2 blame: three items combining caused the accident, moral responsibility and blameworthiness, alpha .85. Study 1 separately rates the health/safety manager, alpha .89; Study 2 explicitly omits manager ratings and adds four experience items, alpha .98. Study 3 uses only moral responsibility/blameworthiness for robot, officer and operator, item correlations .44/.79/.80. Scales range 1–7.
study.models: Studies 1/2 use crossed participant/scenario random intercepts and label slopes with correlated effects, Satterthwaite dfs and 2,000 percentile-bootstrap resamples. Statistical mediation uses joint-significance component tests plus 5,000 quasi-Bayesian simulations. Software permits only one grouping factor per mediation model, so separate participant-only and scenario-only models are reported, not one fully crossed indirect-effect model.
study.study_1: Robot label increases agency b=.27, SE=.05, CI [.16,.37], p<.001, and blame .29, SE=.08, CI [.13,.43], p=.001. Manager contrast .03, SE=.06, CI [−.08,.15], p=.57. Agency/blame r=.41 for machines and .40 for robots. Table 1 agency-to-blame path .57, CI [.45,.70]; residual direct label effect .14, CI [−0.0,.28]. Separate participant/scenario indirect estimates .15 [.08,.23] and .17 [.06,.29].
study.study_2: Unadjusted label contrasts: agency .30 [.19,.40], p<.001; blame .35 [.22,.48], p<.001; experience .01 [−.02,.04], p=.44. Table 1 adjusts for experience and reports agency .28 [.19,.38], total blame .34 [.21,.47], residual direct .17 [.05,.28], and agency-to-blame .54 [.36,.71]. Adjusted/unadjusted differences are not contradictions. Separate participant/scenario indirect estimates .17 [.09,.26] and .20 [.10,.32], both p<.001. Residual direct effect remains significant, so agency is not a demonstrated sole explanation.
study.study_3: Capability package changes sensors/person-object recognition, navigation/target tracking and human oversight. Agency is rated before the harm story: more 4.24 (SD 1.05) versus less 3.15 (1.13), Welch t(275.25)=8.36, p<.001, d=.99. A commander orders an operator to deploy ABTAC; it fires under unclear circumstances, two men are found dead and an injured civilian girl later dies. Robot blame more 3.53 (1.81) versus less 2.95 (1.71), t(280)=2.80, p=.005, d=.33. Officer means 5.02/5.03; operator 4.73/4.90. Target-by-sophistication interaction F(1.47,412.73)=4.75, p=.017, eta-squared=.02 with Greenhouse–Geisser correction. Officer/operator contrasts are nonsignificant. The operator df is printed 79.69; no guessed numerical repair is made.
study.pretest: A separately reported N=45 capability-description pretest (28 women, 17 men; age 36.7, SD 13.76) gives agency 4.41/.89 versus 3.38/1.07, Welch t(36.89)=3.42, p=.002, d=1.05. This is not one of the three main samples or a newly read independent paper.
study.causal_scope: Randomized label/capability packages can identify their total effect on ratings under the design. Agency itself is not independently randomized apart from other capability and oversight information. Reverse blame-to-agency mediation is explicitly untested and dismissed conceptually. Correlation, joint significance and temporal measurement order do not identify a unique causal mediator or prove deserved blame.

summary: No new term. Strengthen existing agency, blame, experience and anthropomorphism entries, with boundary-only notes for agency bias, autonomy and responsibility gaps. Retain floor-limited/null human-blame results and the difference between assigned responsibility and moral truth. Verify two bibliography DOI corrections and one discussion study-number correction without inventing statistical repairs.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.

evidence.quote: Agency encompasses mental abilities such as awareness of self
The more sophisticated robot was assigned

findings.evidence_scope: Three vignette experiments report higher perceived agency for an autonomous-robot label than a machine label, and for a more sophisticated military-robot description. The main retained samples are 145, 143 and 282. Label contrasts are .27 and .30 scale points; the capability-package contrast has d=.99. These are human judgments, not demonstrated robot mental states or validated actual autonomy.
findings.boundary: The label changes both autonomous and robot wording. Study 3 changes sensing, recognition, navigation, target tracking and oversight together. Intentional capacity, independence, control over this accident, consciousness and morally deserved blame remain distinct. Mediation is not identified solely by a significant indirect path.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.
findings.evidence_scope: The label increases the studies 1/2 blame composites by .29/.35 points. In Study 3 the more sophisticated robot receives mean blame 3.53 versus 2.95, d=.33. Human manager/officer/operator contrasts are nonsignificant. Studies 1/2 combine causal contribution, moral responsibility and blameworthiness; Study 3 drops the causal item. The experiment concerns attributed blame, not legal or moral accuracy.
findings.boundary: Causal contribution is not sufficient for deserved blame. Separate ratings do not conserve a fixed blame budget. Increased robot blame does not demonstrate reduced human accountability, real liability transfer, deterrence or a correct answer about machine moral standing.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 measures four experience items and finds a robot/machine contrast b=.01, CI [−.02,.04], p=.44. Ratings lie near the minimum of a 1–7 scale. The authors acknowledge restricted variation may obscure a role for experience in other contexts. Agency remains related to blame after adjustment; that does not establish universal irrelevance of perceived experience.
findings.boundary: A nonsignificant floor-limited contrast is not equivalence or evidence that robots cannot feel. Significant experience/blame correlation for machines but not robots is not itself a significant between-target difference. Human experience attribution, actual feelings and moral patienthood differ.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.

evidence.quote: relying on readily available knowledge of human mental capacities,

findings.evidence_scope: The theoretical account explains robot agency attribution through humanlike mental models, with direct ratings supporting a label/capability effect on perceived agency. Neither visual resemblance nor anthropomorphism as a distinct causal mediator is separately manipulated or isolated. No AI self-report is evaluated.
findings.boundary: Mind attribution is a human response and need not be uniformly mistaken. Labels can convey informative differences. Perceived agency does not establish actual intentions, machine feelings or deception; the study does not uniquely identify stereotyping, automaticity or a single anthropomorphism mechanism.

findings.definition: Inferring an actor's control over an outcome from agency-related cues that do not change the actor's actual control.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.

evidence.quote: described identically and we provided no information

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: matched accident narratives produce different agency judgments under autonomous-robot versus machine wording. However actual control is unspecified and the wording itself can convey relevant capability information. The source says targets could be identical, not that their control was verified identical. This does not independently demonstrate unwarranted agency bias.
findings.boundary: To establish bias, compare inferred control against verified authority/capability held constant. A label-dependent attribution is not automatically an irrational error, and no robot causal-control measurement is supplied.

findings.definition: Judging an entity as able to select and pursue goals or actions independently of external direction.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.

evidence.quote: level of oversight from a human (volition).

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: independence/oversight is one element of a broader sophisticated-capability description. The outcome is a six-item agency composite, including awareness and outcome influence, rather than an isolated autonomy score. Do not count this as a clean test of independence separate from agency.
findings.boundary: Autonomy, task competence, sensor capability, authority and responsibility differ. The intervention bundles them, so a larger composite agency score cannot identify which ingredient changes blame.

findings.definition: A shortfall in the responsibility attributed to actors considered capable of bearing it when an artificial agent is involved in a shared outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The current entry already covers this construct. Add source-specific evidence and boundaries rather than a second label for robot agency or blame.

evidence.quote: Although we found no evidence that autonomy impacts
sponsibility of humans who are responsible for robots

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: Study 1 manager contrast .03, CI [−.08,.15], p=.57; Study 3 officer/operator contrasts p=.96/.38. There is no detected reduction in these human ratings, but no equivalence test, full organizational-chain assessment or fixed-total responsibility allocation. Study 2 omits manager ratings despite a discussion cross-reference to it.
findings.boundary: No detected decrease does not demonstrate zero gap in every setting. More robot blame alone does not prove diminished human blame, nobody accountable, justified exoneration or a real-world accountability gap.

methodological_limits: Convenience internet samples, minimal fictional vignettes and ratings are not actual accident investigations, cultural universals, professional liability findings or demonstrated AI behavior.

The autonomous-robot versus machine phrase changes both category and explicit autonomy. The actual control of the machine is not given, so this is not an isolated robot-word effect or verified control-neutral bias.

Studies 1/2 blame composites include causation, while agency includes outcome influence. Conceptual/measurement overlap may contribute to association. Study 3 removes the causal item but still measures perceived moral responsibility rather than its correctness.

Agency/blame are observed mediators/outcomes. Reverse direction is not tested; separate one-group indirect-effect models do not reproduce a jointly crossed mediation model. Significant residual direct effect in Study 2 excludes a demonstrated sole-agency explanation.

Study 3 changes multiple informative capabilities and oversight together. Its randomized total effect does not isolate agency as a unique causal psychological mechanism, and oversight can legitimately alter perceived duties.

Experience ratings are near the scale minimum, restricting variation. The null label effect is not proof of equal experience judgments, no possible role for feelings or actual lack of machine consciousness. Separate significant/nonsignificant correlations do not test their difference.

Human-blame nulls do not establish exact equivalence, no responsibility gap or no accountability risk in every deployment. Independent ratings are not fixed-total shares and do not directly test a complete institutional responsibility chain.

The article argues retributive/deterrent blame of an unfeeling machine is pointless. That normative premise is not an experimental finding about all functional responsibility, diagnostic attribution, remediation, moral standing or law.

Sensitivity power analyses and described replacement rules do not substitute for preregistered exclusion verification or raw-data reproduction. Cross-study uniqueness and the external supplementary sample remain unknown.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Descriptions of autonomy/sentience can change judgments without establishing actual consciousness or independence. Keep agency, autonomy, experience and warranted responsibility separate.

Distributed responsibility ratings and higher human than machine blame do not alone show diffusion, scapegoating or conserved blame transfer. Here human-label contrasts are null rather than proof of equal responsibility.
Statistical mediation and a plausible normative narrative need separate evaluation. Do not convert ratings, agreement or sensitivity into objectively correct moral judgments.

deferred.reason: Existing agency and blame attribution cover the observed response. A new label would duplicate the construct and overstate a unique mechanism.
Actual control is not verified constant, and autonomy is bundled with capability. Boundary notes clarify these distinctions without new rows or independent behavior-paper credit.

deferred.term: Diffusion / displacement / responsibility gap / moral crumple zone
deferred.reason: No detected human-blame decrease, fixed-total transfer or actual operator scapegoating is demonstrated. Existing gap entry receives only a boundary note.
Theoretical background already overlaps existing entries; the experiments do not independently establish an inverse agent/patient categorization process or a universal theory of morality.

limitations: All eight supplied pages and four figures/two tables were read. External supplements, cited books and full cited primary studies are not claimed read; no author was contacted.
No new row, forced three-paper quota, annual count or automatic ethical/harm edge is introduced. Verified source corrections and unresolved interpretation limits remain explicit.
